title: Their angels (Matthew 18:1–14)
hook: who's the greatest? a child in the middle, and angels before God's face
tomorrow: someone hurt you. where does Jesus say to start?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a coin in a fish: free, and paying anyway, and a faith the size of a seed. Faith moves mountains. Now the disciples have a question of their own.
screen: `FAITH MOVES MOUNTAINS.` → `A QUESTION OF THEIR OWN.`

segments.voice: Greatest of all time: the internet runs that argument every week, about athletes, albums, pizza. The disciples run their version: "Who is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven?" Here's yesterday's question answered. Jesus calls a little child, sets him in the middle of them, and answers with the child. "Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven." They asked who's at the top. He answered who gets in.
screen: `GREATEST OF ALL TIME?` → `A CHILD IN THE MIDDLE.` → `NOT WHO'S TOP: WHO GETS IN.`

segments.voice: Then the line this day is named for: "Take heed that ye despise not one of these little ones; for I say unto you, That in heaven their angels do always behold the face of my Father which is in heaven." Their angels. Christians read those two words in more than one way, and both readings have a real case. Catholics and Orthodox Christians speak of guardian angels, and the Catholic Catechism points to this verse: Jesus says the little ones have angels of their own, and he says it plainly, in the present tense. Why explain it away? Some Protestant readers hold the verse more lightly. Angels are real to them too, but they hear this as a picture of nearness: the people nobody notices are the ones closest to God's face. Build a whole teaching on one verse, they say, and you may say more than Jesus did. Notice where both sides end up, though. Neither lets anyone look down on a child. And Jesus goes straight on to a shepherd with a hundred sheep who leaves the ninety and nine to find one that wandered. "Even so it is not the will of your Father which is in heaven, that one of these little ones should perish."
screen: `TAKE HEED: DESPISE NOT ONE.` · `GUARDIAN ANGELS: TAKE IT AS SAID.` · `A PICTURE OF NEARNESS.` · `THE SHEPHERD LEAVES THE NINETY-NINE.` · then, large: `THEIR ANGELS SEE GOD.`

segments.voice: Find a photo of yourself as a small child, or bring one to mind: the haircut, the shoes, the expression. Look at that face for the length of the sit, without grading it. Then let your eyes rest on one child you know now, in a photo or in memory, and look at them the same way.
Their angels. Jesus' words for the little ones' angels, who always behold the Father's face.
Something to keep: their angels see God, and nobody is too small to be watched over. Day done.

howItsDone: Catholic and Orthodox Christians speak of guardian angels and some teach children a short prayer to their angel; other Christians read Matthew 18:10 as a picture of God's closeness to the small.

fork.setup: your friend says 'their angels' is just a picture of God's nearness, nothing more. state the other side's best case.
options: Jesus says plainly that the little ones have angels of their own, before God.
the verse names each child's angel and lists what it does all day.
every church has always taught it the same way, so it settles it.
fork.reveal: the guardian-angel reading rests on the words themselves: their angels, in heaven, always beholding God's face. the other side reads the same words as nearness. both refuse to despise a little one.

chat.says: helping with kids' choir. a six-year-old asked if she has her own angel. what do i say??
options: Jesus said little ones have angels who see God’s face. Churches explain it differently.
Say yes, and the Bible gives her angel's name and tells you what it does.
Say no, angels are only a picture, so there's nothing watching over her.
chat.meaning: Matthew 18:10: their angels always behold the Father's face. Some churches teach guardian angels from it; others hear nearness. Both say she matters.

Catechism.meaning: a book that sets out a church's teaching, here the Catholic one

Orthodox.meaning: the Eastern Orthodox churches, with roots in the early Greek-speaking church

guardian angels.meaning: angels believed to watch over each person, in Catholic and Orthodox teaching

ninety and nine.meaning: the King James way to say ninety-nine
